plots.name: Onset vs day — the zeitgeber steps, the rhythm ramps

notes.text: WORKFLOW: transients after a phase shift. A transient is one of the intermediate cycles a rhythm passes through between the shift of the zeitgeber and the re-attainment of a steady-state phase. Both records here get an 8 h shift on the same day, one an ADVANCE and one a DELAY, and the zeitgeber steps instantly in both; neither rhythm does. The advance closes its 8 h at about 1 h per cycle (roughly 8 transient cycles), the delay at about 1.5 h per cycle (roughly 6) — the standard asymmetry, and the reason eastward travel costs more days than westward. Read the onset plot next to the actograms: grey is the imposed schedule, coloured is the biology, and the horizontal gap between them IS the transient. Two consequences. First, only the phase measured after transients have subsided is the steady-state shift, so a PRC must be scored from post-transient cycles. Second, transients are diagnostic: a record that jumps straight to the new schedule is being DRIVEN by it (see the masking card), whereas one that crawls is a genuine oscillator re-entraining. Classically (Pittendrigh) the pacemaker itself resets within about a cycle, so the crawl reflects a lag between the overt rhythm and the pacemaker in a hierarchical, multi-oscillator system; the modern counterpart is the SCN resetting quickly while peripheral clocks in liver, lung and muscle take several cycles (Yamazaki et al. 2000; Reddy et al. 2002; Yamanaka et al. 2008).
